utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before calling your next witness, Mr. Mundis, I would like to return to an issue that we dealt with last week, that was the admission of a report which was proposed by the Prosecution to be an expert report and where the Defence objected against using it as an expert report, mainly on the basis that this report was not drafted on the request of the Tribunal or of the OTP, and reference was made by the Defence to the Kunarac case, arguing that in the Kunarac case, the report of Professor Cleiren, which is written, C-l-e-i-r-i-n - although it is wrongly spelled in the Kunarac transcript - that in the Kunarac case, that it would not have been admitted into evidence. Since last Thursday, the Chamber tried to find the exact spot, and we did find the discussion on the admissibility of the testimony and of an expert report of Professor Cleiren on pages 4154 and following, that is -- I think it was the 29th of May - I am not quite sure about that - and then it continued on the 30th of May, of the year 2000. Having looked at it, we do not find any reference to who ordered the drafting of the report. As a matter of fact, we noticed that there had been a great debate on whether the factual basis of the report stemmed from the personal knowledge, the personal observations, of Professor Cleiren, rather than the question whether the report was drafted on the request of the Tribunal or the OTP. And no decision has been taken, as far as I can see, because on the 30th of May of the year 2000, finally the Prosecution has withdrawn its intent to call Professor Cleiren as a witness. So, is this the part of the Kunarac transcript you were referring to or is there any other source, because we had some difficulties in linking this part of the transcript to the argument raised by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was at the time that it was, 29th, 30th of May, 2000, and there was a discussion on the admissibility of the testimony of Professor Cleiren. Formally speaking, there was no decision of the Tribunal. They never reached a decision after the Prosecution withdrew their proposal to tender it. The point of the debate of this discussion was that the Mrs. Cleiren did not give her opinion and findings. It was not done on the request of any party or the Trial Chamber. As far as we understood at the time, Professor Cleiren was supposed to testify on the circumstances as a member of the Bosinas [phoen] Commission, checking the data and gathering the data for a certain period of time, and it was a question of rape. So formally, the decision was never reached. But our stand is that if the Prosecution withdrew their proposal after the debate, I am not sure whether that was Judge Hunt's opinion, but the point is that Professor Cleiren never gave her opinion or findings at anyone's request. And this is -- the Defence accepted this and that was one of the reasons why we didn't object. So in our statement, the reasons, we said that Mr. Zecevic didn't give his opinion, it wasn't his findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is a different argument from who ordered the report to be drafted, because when I did understand and when the Chamber does understand the argument well, it was mainly on the basis whether the report was drafted on the request of the local authorities in Sarajevo rather than on request -- at the request of the Tribunal. But that is not an issue as far as we can see in the debate before the Trial Chamber presided by Judge Hunt. Judge Hunt was mainly putting questions, but I am corrected to the extent that Judge Mumba was presiding. But at least this is the part of the transcript you relied upon when objecting against the admission of a report of, at least, of an expert -- of the expert Mr. Zecevic testifying in this court. I must say, to testify in this court. Thank you very much. Then having clarified this issue, Mr. Mundis, your next witness we will be Colonel Kolp, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please bring the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, there is one question that we are interested in still, more and more: When is the Prosecution going to be able to tell us about the pieces and because there are certain questions we would like to ask every time a witness comes, and we don't know when that is going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When You are talking about the pieces, you are talking about the shrapnel pieces?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you call the "grattage." You heard the question, Mr. Mundis, but let's first proceed. Good afternoon. Colonel Kolp, as far as I understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is my name, Mr. President, but unfortunately, I am not yet a Colonel. I am a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From your answer, I take it that you do understand me in a language -- that you hear me in a language you understand, Mr. Kolp .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. Of course I understand French, that is my mother tongue, but I also understand English and I can speak it, but I would say that if I am speaking about such important things, I would prefer to use my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you prefer to speak in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will express myself in English, usually. Mr. Kolp, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration, and the text will be handed out to you now by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by counsel by the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Colonel, you are currently serving in the Belgian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long have you been in the Belgian army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I entered the service in 1973, September 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which branch of the Belgian army do you have the bulk of your service?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: It was in the infantry and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were assigned under the flag of the United Nations to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, I volunteered for this mission. That was at the end of year 1992, and I was -- I started in March 1993 and I stayed there November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in which part of Bosnia were you stationed during that period from March 1993 through November 1994?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: In fact, most of my time, I was in the Sarajevo sector which was comprised of obviously the Sarajevo zone and its variants and also central Bosnia, more specifically, the Kiseljak region where I was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this period, where was the office that you held, where did you physically go to work in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: From the second day of my mission, I was working at the HQ of the Sarajevo sector as a liaison officer between the BH command, or for the BH command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And was the headquarters of the Sarajevo sector located in the PTT building in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, it was. So the HQ was located in the PTT building and my base was with the HQ at the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am sorry, but on page 5, line 5, I know that the transcript will be corrected but this witness didn't say that he was based in Kiseljak, but that he depended on Kiseljak. That is what I understood that he said in his mother tongue that resembles mine, so I believe there is an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Attention will be paid to your observation while working on the transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, what were your primary duties as the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: This was a task of several facets, but the most important task was to have a communication or liaison with the BH command, so with the BH commander, specifically General Morillon, but that didn't go for very long and then General Briquemont, whom I knew for a longer time, and then finally General Rose and the Sarajevo sector, which was on the level of the main staff, was mostly staffed by the French. The second task was to solicit from the municipal Bosnia Serb authorities to ask authorization for a passage of convoys: Military convoys, UN convoys or NGO convoys, humanitarian convoys, and so on. And to this is also added a liaison mission between these two HQS on one side, the sector Sarajevo on the other side, BH command, and also the warring parties. This is at the time of the war. These were my principal tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say "the warring parties," which parties are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Most of the time was spent on the Bosnian Serbs but it also happened that I met Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently would you meet with authorities of the Bosnia Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Since the problem of convoys was very important, to start with, I saw them every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where would you meet with the Bosnian Serb authorities, at what physical location would you meet with them?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: The location was Lukavica, where their main staff was, the HQ of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was there one primary Bosnian Serb officer that you dealt with in your capacity as the liaison officer or did you meet with many different authorities at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No, the main person was Major Indic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently would you meet with Major Indic?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Practically every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what were the primary subject matters that you discussed with Major Indic during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: The main subject from my side, of course, was obtaining clearance or authorization for the passage of convoys, mainly speaking, through Central Bosnia, Kiseljak Sarajevo, through two checkpoints, Sierra 1 at Kobiljaca and Sierra 4 at Kasindolska Cesta between Ilidza and Sarajevo. And, of course, as a liaison officer, all specific communications from different commanders, from the BH commander and the sector Sarajevo commander, was then sent to the local commanders, so this went through Colonel Indic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have referred in your testimony to both Major Indic and Colonel Indic. Is that in fact one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I spoke about Colonel Indic because he was rapidly promoted, but I always called him Commander Indic or Major Indic. But he was promoted to Colonel very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was Major or Lieutenant-Colonel Indic's offices located in the headquarters of the Bosnian Serb army at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. The headquarters of this corps of the 1st Sarajevo Romanija Corps was located in Lukavica, and Major Indic had his office in the building of the HQ, which was located a couple of dozen metres away from the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if General Galic also had his office in the same building?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was General Galic's office in relation to Major Indic's office?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: At the time when I was there, the office of General Galic was located about 20 metres away from the office of Major Indic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what Major Indic's responsibilities within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps consisted of?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. It is a little complex in the sense that the Major Indic was, I think - that is what I believe - he was a key person. He had to coordinate everything that was coming from the outside, meaning the United Nations the UNMOs, the military, the humanitarian organisations, the NGOs. Everywhere that there was a problem or which was particularly sensitive to have problems, everything went through the office of Major Indic. I also believed that he was a coordinator and a direct associate of the commander of the Serbian Army Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which commander are you referring to, when you say, "the commander of the Serbian army Corps"?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Here we are talking about General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience with Major Indic, do you know if he in fact reported to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I think, I believe, that Major Indic depended on General Galic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "depended on General Galic," do you mean to say that he reported information that you provided to him up the chain of command to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, in a part of the Bosnian Serb army, the chain of command was very rigid: A head is a head, a chief is a chief. He would not accept that something else should be done opposite to what he said, although every chief had some initiatives that he could take, but as far as the most important things were concerned, it is clear that the General knew in any case, since Major Indic had to report to him on a regular basis, about what was going on. And I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of issues did you take to Major Indic for action as a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: These were, to start with, or even throughout the mission, the first point would be asking for authorization for passages of convoys, then various complaints that came from the HQ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, meaning, the UNHQ, which were addressed to the military authorities of the Bosnian Serb when they came from either General Briquemont, General Morillon or General Rose. This was mostly addressed to General Mladic through the chain of command. But also, when there were complaints that came from the Sarajevo sector, the level of the commander of Sarajevo sector, his equivalent was General Galic. This was the first thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little bit about the authorization for passages of convoys. Can you give us some concrete examples as to what type of authorisation you were seeking from Major Indic?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, we had to, in principle, address at first verbally and then, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. if it didn't get any better, we would have to do it in writing. It would be 24 or 48 hours in advance. These were always problems with the delays, and in order to have these military convoys, UN convoys, pass, most of them had right of passage without being checked, but that was never enforced. Or the convoys, humanitarian convoys that were bringing either medicine, medical equipment and materiel, perhaps sometimes food, water, because at a certain point Sarajevo, in fact, had no water for four years and also every now and then, but we tried to get the situation to become better. But basically these were -- this was equipment that the Serbs considered to be sensitive and that is why they wouldn't allow it to go through. But what really happened is that there were negotiation, and following these negotiations, the level of the medical materiel, the needs was felt in both parts, camps, in both parties, so these convoys were able to get into the town, at least one part, and then another part of the convoy went to another part, to the hospital between the airport and Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you requested assistance from Major Indic with respect to these convoys, was that assistance forthcoming after you made such requests?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, we can say that this depended on the situation. In general, it was always very difficult, very complex, to get authorisation, and this meant that in most of the cases, we saw that there was refusal and we had to send a message through another chain of command to Pale to the HQ. There was one period it happened, there was a short period that -- there were periods which were less difficult than others, but in fact it was never easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there some instances where you requested specific action of Major Indic and that those requests were then met?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. Following the question that you asked me a few moments ago, I also asked about other requests directly to Major Indic and on several occasions, four or five occasions, we asked for him to stop the shellings, the bombardments, and in particular, in certain locations, to stop the sniping activity which, in general, had as a response the fact that it continued. It was only on one or two occasions after a certain time because it was always a long time needed to go -- to take it through the chain of command and, on two occasions, there were positive results. But that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These one or two occasions that you referred to, do they refer to shelling requests or sniping requests or both?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, that pertained to both. I think that it happened a total of five times, both when we are talking about sniping activities and the shelling. Therefore, I intervened every time this was addressed, either to the Sarajevo sector or the BH command. And naturally, when the result was not positive, we had to apply to another level of hierarchy and start negotiations there, be it between sector Sarajevo directly or General Soubirou, or somebody who was a member of his staff, or be it to the BH command. We would apply either to General Milanovic or General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Major Indic had the authority to halt the sniping or the shelling when you requested him to do so?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to intervene because if we are to phrase this question in this way, then we will not know actually what geographical area this question pertain to. We know that the armies are divided into sectors and so on, so could Mr. Mundis please make his question more precise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...area, Mr. Mundis. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just in order for me not to interrupt Mr. Mundis once again, could he also give a time delineation to his question, because as we were able to see, various military leaders had various -- held various ranks. So could he be more precise, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, let's first focus on roughly the first six months that you were in Sarajevo, that is from roughly March through September of 1993. During that period, do you recall whether you made any requests to Major Indic to stop sniping or to stop shelling?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, that did happen, especially when it comes to the notorious bombing of Stup. If I remember, it was in October or November of 1993. At that time the negotiations were being held in Geneva, if I am not mistaken, Bosnian or, rather, Muslim delegation was in Geneva, or that could have been New York. I don't remember the name of the person who presided over the Presidency at that time. That person exerted pressure and insisted on stopping the shelling. However, there came about the intervention of General Briquemont, and as a result of that, we had temporary ceasefire, armistice, and as far as I am concerned, on three occasions, I had an opportunity to lodge a complaint with General Indic, a complaint about shelling and sniping incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a translation error, but I heard you refer to General Indic. Again, are you referring to General Indic or Major Indic?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Major. Major Indic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate dates or month during which you made complaints directly to Major Indic regarding sniping or shelling?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, it is quite difficult for me to remember now. I believe it was in late 1993 or early 1994. I would say that during that period of time, this military activity was quite intense. During the entire time I was there, as you know, there were sniping incidents and shelling, so I can't remember exactly whether this was in mid 1993, late 1993 or early 1994. It is difficult for me to pinpoint it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what geographic areas your complaints were made with reference to?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. This was -- first, we had the Nedzarici zone. That area is located behind the Oslobodjenje newspaper building. If I can say between the Stup bridge and behind it. So this is quite an important location. And this also took place in Grbavica and in the Jewish cemetery. I know the southern part much better than the northern because I travelled through the southern part much more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you ever in Major Indic's office when he issued any type of orders with respect to shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question seems to be a leading one to me, Mr. President, and I don't think that it should be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Major Indic's office, did you ever hear him issue any type of orders to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Actually, that happened on one occasion. I was present when an order was issued. It was not issued in English or French, but rather in Serbo-Croatian. I speak only a few words of Serbo-Croatian, and my assistant who was present at the time interpreted it quickly for me and said that it was an order for shooting. I tried to learn something more about it but the French soldier, who was a member of the Foreign Legion, would not tell me anything more about it. This is simply strictly what I heard myself. However, I couldn't understand what was being said in Serbo-Croatian because I don't speak that language. However, when on another occasion I personally lodged in a request, I heard that a mortar fired -- had fired in the Lukavica area -- in the Grbavica area, I apologise. I was with Major Indic at the time and he at the time told me, "Well, there will be a few Muslims less now." I don't know whether it was a joke or not, however, I thought it was in poor taste.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many times did you hear outgoing mortar fire while you were at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: While I was in Lukavica, I heard only once that rounds had been fired from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any time while you were in Lukavica, were there any incoming mortar or artillery shells of any kind to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No. While I was present in Lukavica, it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the times that you were at Major Indic's office, did you ever see any other visitors or guests or people who were coming to see him?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, there were many visitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hesitated. However, in the French transcript, there is no details concerning the type of artillery shells that were used, and I would like for this to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, do you know the approximate time period when you were at Lukavica when you heard the outgoing mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No, I couldn't give you any dates with precision. I don't want to mislead you and therefore I would rather not answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, you just indicated a few moments ago that there were many visitors to Major Indic's office. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what types of visitors and who some of these people were, if you knew?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. There were many visitors. I have already said that, on one hand, there were many representatives of the United Nations, be it civilian services of the UN or the representatives of the commander of chief of the Sarajevo sector, Colonel Valentin. There were also people from the engineering corps who were in charge of everything that had to be with utilities, energy companies, electrical companies, gas companies, and so on. There were also liaison officers such as myself, and there were also UN observers there. On the other hand, we had soldiers of the VRS, and on many occasions there were members of the paramilitary formations present there as well. Those must have been some special units that had a skull, a human skull design on their badge. On their hats they had this human skull design, however, this doesn't prove anything. My assistant who knew them quite well, told me that -- told me the following: "Major, do not speak to these people, they are very dangerous."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who any of these "very dangerous people" were?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them personally. I knew, of course, that such formations existed. In majority of the cases, we called them "uncontrolled elements." We used that term to describe them. However, I suppose that every person in charge had to know what was going on in their sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time frame when you saw these people in Major Indic's office?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, I think that I saw them on several occasions, and I would say that it was sometime between April or May of 1993 until early 1994 at the latest. I didn't see them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you be more specific with respect to your statement that you saw them on "several occasions." Approximately how many occasions, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, I must have seen them some three or four times. But when I say, "I saw them," that means it was just in passing. I did not have any physical contact with them. I did not talk to them. I simply observed them. Of course, when you have any kind of task of this nature, it is up to you to report to your superiors what you had seen and I reported to my superiors that I had seen them, and this was within the scope of my responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if the people that you saw on three or four times were the same people or were they different people?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No, no. On two occasions, I saw one or two persons from that group, therefore, I think that on two occasions, I saw the same persons. But then on other occasions, there were different persons. However, every time there were people from the same kind of paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of clothing were these people wearing?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, I didn't consider them soldiers because soldiers have to wear uniforms or something that is like a uniform. These people had various kinds of civilian clothes on them, perhaps some military jackets on top of it. And then they had a typical cap that one can see in the Slav countries. It was a black cap. And those were typically the clothes of some paramilitary formations. Some had a skull on their caps. However, I did not consider that to be uniform. For me, these people were not soldiers in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did these people have any characteristic hair style or facial hair of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to object. The witness just now said something different than what we can see in the French transcript. These people were not soldiers in uniform and this witness said, "For me, these people were not soldiers. They were not soldiers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what my recollection as well, but perhaps, Mr. Mundis, we could clarify the issue so in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding: whether or not they were soldiers in uniforms or whether they are not soldiers and that they had no, I would say, proper uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, did any of these people wear any type of military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: They had parts of uniforms, whether it was a jacket or trousers. In addition to that, they had plain civilian clothes like a jean jacket. So they did not have a full uniform similar to some other uniforms that I saw in other units. So these were not typical real uniforms. However, I have to add that -- that everybody, be it is teenager or an elderly person, had some kind of a weapon and some kind of uniform on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did these people that you saw have military-style haircuts or did they have -- can you describe their hair and/or facial hair, if any?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, they did not have what one might call a military haircut. They had long hair and beards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have described these people as being part of paramilitary formations. How do you know that if they weren't wearing uniforms of any kind?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, the situation there was quite peculiar, as you probably know, in view of the fact that -- that the Serbian army in Bosnia had a large number of artillery weapons and tanks, but had, however, very few infantry troops. Their life was quite difficult. When they tried to gain territory in Sarajevo in order to put that sector under their control, since it is a mountain region, I think that they had to compensate for the insufficiency of their troops with the soldiers that I myself call paramilitary. So it was not militia but what I called paramilitary formations. So from our point of view and not from a Yugoslav point of view, from our point of view, we called these people Chetniks. So they were extreme nationalists, and this is how I would describe them. This is now my personal opinion. I think that they were subordinated to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. There were some other corps there as well, but let us not go into that now, because that is not what we are focussing on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What makes you think that these people were subordinated to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: These people were what I call uncontrollable elements, or elements out of control. I came to this conclusion based on these visits. As I said, I did not see many of those visits or visitors, but I did see some. The person that was my assistant used to meet them quite often, and these people came regularly visit Major Indic, so I believe that there was some kind of exchange of information between them and it is possible that they received orders, or at the request of their superiors, they engaged in certain tasks. However, I couldn't say more about this because I had no direct contacts with them. I can't tell you that these people went to see such and such in order to get orders. As you know, when -- I know that everybody had -- was armed. Everybody had weapons on them, however, the weapons that they had on them at the time were not something that was typical that one could see anyplace, any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of weapons did they have on them?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, they had typical Kalasnikovs, which one can see everywhere. It is a weapon that practically everybody used there at the time. However, they also had very modern rifles. I saw some assault rifles and other quite modern equipment that one cannot encounter easily. We know that in that area there were so much arms trafficking that one could find any kinds of weapons. However, the weapons that they had were not easily obtained even there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Major --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. The classic type, what I heard the major say was not at all interpreted by the English booth. It is not at all in the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so I take it that working on the transcript, especially on page 21, line 7, that proper attention will be paid to it. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you in need of the translations of these words, because they are not only not in the transcript, but -- I didn't listen to the English translation, as a matter of fact. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, do you remember if any of these people were escorted by VRS personnel in the Lukavica barracks or if they were simply roaming freely?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No, they were not escorted. They were moving freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Major Indic about these paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience during the time you were in Sarajevo, how much authority did Major Indic have?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: As far as I know or I understand, Major Indic was a key person who was supposed to, as far as I understand, who was supposed to report for all of his actions to his chief, who was the commander of the corps, of the army corps. At the time that was General Galic. However, I have to also say that -- consider that I am a soldier myself. Every chief has a chain of command in his area of action and some initiative; he has some room for some initiative, and Major Indic probably did that. But I think that that was on as far as he could in a very rigid structure, and in spite of a very respectful chain of command of the Serb military, which at that time was their force, their strength, I think that it was very difficult not to report to the chief. And, again, I don't know of any army where you do not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, as part of your duties during the period that you were in Sarajevo, did you also have the opportunity to intermingle with the civilian population of the city?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I met civilian population everywhere: In the city, on the Serb side, on the Croat side, and where I still know a large number of people. As far as the events are concerned in the city, yes, I met many people. There is one thing that I would like to stress, however, is that the siege of anything whatsoever, of any fortress in the medieval times, and here with a city with 500.000 inhabitants, it is sometimes very difficult, very hard, to see the suffering of the population the way that they have suffered. And personally, this is what I feel, I personally cannot understand how when you are attacking civilians, that you are then -- that you have a fighting between the militaries, that is one thing, and it is true there is no such thing as a clean war. But I have had many contacts with civilians and I have -- through a chain of my own personal acquaintances, I helped people in food - this is not important for this case - but I helped schools and children. I did it everywhere, not just in the city, but also on the Serb side, but much more in the city because the proportions were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber the effect of the sniping campaign on the population of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot accept that we ask this -- that this question is asked, "sniping campaign," as we are contesting that there was a sniping campaign. We cannot accept this, the way it is phrased, because of its form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained because, until now, there has been no testimony to any sniping campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were in Sarajevo, did you become aware of any incidents involving snipers?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I saw for myself on a regular basis. I can't tell you about their frequency because it was everyday life. After all, to hear an isolated shot in certain parts of the city, well, it is clear that I also saw reports. So I heard and saw for myself these incidents and I was myself on several occasions the target of isolated snipers. They may have been Serb. I am saying a supposed target, because it is very hard to say where it comes from. As far as I am concerned, when I was in the centre of the city, this came from the neighbourhoods that I told you a moment ago. But it was, yes, it was regular. I could say that this was part of everyday life, practically. The reports that were also mentioned, so the reports that arrived to the HQ of the UN also mentioned these incidents. But I have personally lived through them and I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Mr. President, but I have to be very precise with the transcript. What I heard this witness say a moment ago was that "supposedly Serb" because there were several Serbs. But, in English, it says, "a supposed target." This is not at all the same thing. And the witness said, "supposedly Serb."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...on the other hand, on page 24, line 7, it says: "They may have been Serb."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but just afterwards. Just after that, the witness said in French - we can ask him to repeat - "supposedly Serb" because he wasn't sure about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...but from the other part of the testimony, it becomes clear that the witness had difficulties in identifying those who sniped were of Serbian positions. He just referred, I would say, in rather general words to the areas of the city where, in his view, the sniping came from. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But it is -- it would be helpful if it was more precise in relation to the French transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very will. Care will be taken of it. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, based on your encounters with the civilian population in Sarajevo, do you have an opinion as to how these sniping incidents affected them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the question asked by Mr. Mundis [In English] "incidents." [Interpretation] Is Mr. Mundis talking about all the sniping incidents, that we cannot determine where they came from, or one specific incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start, Commander Kolp, with sniping incidents in general. Are you aware of sniping being conducted by both parties?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, I will try and be clearer. As far as I am concerned, when I was targeted by a sniper, it was impossible to say, in most cases, where this came from. That is as far as I am concerned because -- and this is -- I want to remain honest and say fair that what also existed is that there was provocation to make believe that there was another party that was firing at the UN. And it is important to say that when a sniper really wanted to hit me, I think he would have done it. As far as the local population is concerned -- I have to cut my answer in two. As far as the local population is concerned, the objective was clear, is to create a climate of terror and atmosphere of terror in the centre of the city, to make people feel on the edge. And when this was coming, in particular, as far as I am concerned, from the Grbavica area, it wasn't difficult because that came from the other side of the river, buildings on the other side of the river and the area called the Jewish cemetery; it was clear that we knew where it was coming from. I have to say that there was a team, I was present, that when we wanted, and this happened in 1994, when they wanted to restore the tramline going more or less up to Oslobodjenje building. So, what happened, there was this street that was going there called "the sniper alley" or "the sniper avenue" where it was very easy -- near Nedzarici. It was very easy to have it covered by sniper fire. And Major Indic himself had said that if containers were placed in that location to protect that part of the sniper alley, so the snipers coming from Nedzarici, they would fire. And so we went to place these containers. We had just placed the first container, and "we" meaning the UN force, with the APCs, opposite the Nedzarici, there in that street, and a Ukrainian soldier of the UN was trying to move the crane and he was then targeted. He was fired on. He was very -- he was in a great state of shock. He went underground and there was an order to the French units to fire in order to evacuate the area. The area was evacuated. The containers were never placed, but I can state here that snipers' fire came from the Nedzarici area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, during the time that you are talking about right now, which party controlled the Nedzarici area?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, I never had a contact with the local commander. That was a local commander who was supposed to, as far as I believe, who was supposed to give orders to the subordinates of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I never met him. This was a local commander. And he was reporting, obviously, to this area, of the area of responsibility. It was in the area of responsibility of this army corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps my question wasn't clear. Which army controlled the Nedzarici area at the time of the incident you have just described?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Nedzarici was under the control of the VRS, that is, the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, as part of your duties and responsibilities particularly with respect to the convoy operations, did you regularly visit the marketplaces in Sarajevo to determine quantities of foodstuffs?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. It is important to know that at a given time. I had an additional task at the Sarajevo sector area, which was -- to do, and this was my responsibility, to go on a regular basis to take the temperature of the population, so to speak, to check the situation at the markets, meaning to see the prices, the food that is being sold, the material that is being sold, and this was one of the minor elements to have, to be aware of, to be as an indication, first of all, of what is coming into town, how it is going into town, and also to check the morale of the population. These were all elements which helped us establish a view. So I regularly went to check the prices, and these were all little elements, like elements to a puzzle, and it all went towards the top and the top, the leadership, was then able to conduct an analysis, hoping that this was correct, evaluating, assessing the situation in the population, the humanitarian side, to find out what was the state of the spirit of the population. So it did happen, I regularly did it, I regularly did a round of all the markets in Sarajevo

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the late start, were you still intending on breaking at the normal time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We usually have a break after one hour and a half. Since we started late, I was thinking at about, well, within five minutes to have a break. But if you could find a suitable moment to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask is that perhaps this is a suitable moment. I think the next line of questions will take a little bit longer than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, right before the break, you were describing for the Trial Chamber how part of your duties involved visiting various marketplaces in Sarajevo. Were you, in fact, in Sarajevo on the day the Markale market was shelled?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was in Sarajevo at that time and on that day. I was in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far from the Markale market were you at the time of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, more or less I could say, as the crow flies, about 200 metres -- 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were you doing at the time of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, it was one of those days when I was doing what I was -- I was doing my town rounds. I had first gone to the market, which is a little bit before Zetra, at the beginning of the road that goes up to the Kosevo hospital. And then I had left for the centre of the city, the town, and I must have been from the wrong -- on the other side of the cathedral, there is a pedestrian area or street actually that goes to the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what you heard on that day.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: What I heard when I was there was a rather strong explosion, but it was a bit muted because you have quite of few buildings apparently between where I now know as the Markale market and where I was. I heard an explosion. But from the buildings, I say as the crow flies, I was some ways away and I was cut off by the buildings. And so it was a more muted sound. But it was a shell falling somewhere, that you could hear, that is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date or the approximate date of this incident?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: It was in February in 1994, and if I am not mistaken, it must have been the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you heard one explosion or more than one explosion on that day?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No. I just heard one explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you do after you heard that explosion?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, you know, when something happens and you are not very far from what is happening, you see people running in every direction. And so I went over toward where the sound was coming from, the place where the people were coming from. A lot of people were shouting. And I arrived a little bit later. There were bodies spread out just about everywhere. There were wounded people. There was screaming. Anything that could be driven was used as an ambulance, and afterwards, two ambulances of the French forces whose were there on site from the United Nations, they were armoured ambulances, they assisted in transporting the wounded people, those that were the most seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall from the time when you first heard the explosion until you arrived at the Markale market, approximately how much time elapsed?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, it is hard to answer that question because you know at that time, you know time was very -- passing very quickly, but it wasn't very long. I should tell you also that I was being pretty careful when I moved over there because you never know what you are going to come up against or what might happen. Maybe 5, 10 minutes. It is not a lot, but it is a lot at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall as you were making your way to the Markale market whether you saw any ABiH military formations or military equipment of any kind?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, listen, you know, the first thing you have to know is that in the city everybody who was a fighting agent, who could defend the town against the Serbian opposition, had to put on a uniform. Whoever didn't have a uniform on was looked for. That was one thing. What I could tell you is that there were no military unit or armed soldiers, specifically, at that location. And so you should know that the Markale market is a very small place and the shops are right next to one another. It is the place -- well, it is not the largest market, but in terms of people, in numbers of people, it is the largest. Everybody was crowded together, pressed up against one another. To answer your question, I would say there was no specific military -- military objective at that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say, "there was no specific military objective at that particular point," what point are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, the Markale market is a market like you see everywhere in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the world. I say it is a place where everybody knows exactly that there is a lot -- there are a lot of the people and that is a place you could find some food or something of everything. There was really this and that. And every day the market was overbrimming with people. That doesn't mean that there wasn't a person here or there wearing military clothes or who had gone out to do some shopping. As I said, everyone who was young enough, even young people who could wear the uniform was in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you saw any significant military presence on the market that day when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No. No, there weren't very many soldiers. I wouldn't even say that it happened, but I can tell you there are place where ordinarily you would see soldiers because it was either soldiers who were on leave or on the front line. Ordinarily, they wouldn't be walking around the market. I didn't really see any more people -- any more soldiers at that point than at any other point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, at the time of the shelling of the Markale market, you had been in the Belgian army for more than 20 years, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as an infantry officer, had you trained and/or worked with mortars during the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. As a military person and an infantry person, I would say as a chief, I wasn't a mortar specialist but I had assistants who were. But I did have to be familiar with certain things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall on the day the Markale market was shelled, whether you heard any type of mortar being launched as contrasted with hearing a mortar shell landing?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, if you are asking whether I heard from where it came from or heard the part it was leaving, no. If you are asking whether I heard the explosion, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really very sorry to have to come back to this. But in English it says "from where it came." And he said that the departure, the departure point, which is not the same thing at all. The witness said I didn't hear any departure -- any shots being fired as opposed to where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...also the translation should be something like "I didn't hear it being fired" or something like that, but not from where it came. I assume the proper care will be taken with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have been asked, in order to make more certain that these things are clarified, that I would rather ask the witness to repeat what he -- what his testimony was. So, therefore, Commander Kolp, could you please repeat your answer to the question -- well, you heard the whole discussion about it. But could you nevertheless repeat the answer you gave. You may do it in your own language, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I would recall that the explosion, I heard it. I heard it arrive. But its departure, when I say "departure," by that I mean the place where the weapon was fired which was going to project the shell to its target. Therefore, when I say, "depart," departure, that is the point from which the shot was fired, I did not hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one thing: This is, as far as I understand, not just a repetition of your answer, but it adds something, because, as far as I remember, you said in French that you didn't here "le depart" and now you add something, that you say you didn't hear the "il y a des endroits qui different."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but of course if I didn't hear the departure, then I can confirm what I said before. For your information, if I don't hear anything, then it is not possible to locate just like that, right then and there, the very place where the shot might have been -- the mortar shot might have been fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. So your testimony is that you did not hear the mortar being fired and, therefore, hearing nothing. Your ears could not assist you in identifying a spot from where it might have been fired. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you permit me, Your Honour, that is what I said. However, you probably know better than I that for months, and even more perhaps, some people continued to have doubts as to the exact departure points, the exact location, from where the mortar shot originated, even though you talk about Markovici. It was north -- the shell was fired north of -- from the north. But there are observers from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't hear it being launched, so your ears cannot assist us. I am not asking for any assistance, but I am just trying to understand your testimony well and what others are thinking about a source of fire is a totally different thing. You have no knowledge about that; is that correct? I see you nodding "yes." For the transcript, nodding is always a bit of a problem, Commander Kolp. So I see you are nodding "yes." Please proceed, Mr. Stamp -- Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, were there ever times when -- let me withdraw that. Commander Kolp, during the time you were stationed in Sarajevo, where did you sleep at nighttime?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I had my bases in the PTT building, although frequently, outside during -- somewhere else during the day and often at night, but my base was at the PTT building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you ever present in the PTT building when that building came under mortar attack?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to say, and I maintain what I said, the Bosnian Serbs, that is the Bosnian Serb army, had very good artillery people, and the building was probably more out of intimidation because there was no physical damage or casualties. It was hit exactly where it had to be, and that is why I say -- if I haven't said it, I am going to say it, that is why I say it, that, after all, that when a city is under siege, people -- the people who are besieging in the city, they are familiar with it. They know very well where they have to fire, when they have to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And as a military person, would there be any advantages that would accrue from being familiar with the city?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this question is being asked, were the two armies -- well, there are two armies that were familiar with the city. Both the armies were familiar with the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are wondering why the question is asked, or is that what I understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I wanted to know is if we are speaking about one of the two armies or if we are speaking about both of them because both armies were familiar with the city and both could fire. They were in-going and outgoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's clarify the question. It reads in English: "And as a military person, would that be any advantages that would accrue from being familiar with the city?" So Mr. Piletta-Zanin wonders to whom you are referring, perhaps being both parties that were familiar with the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a general rule, Commander Kolp, during the time you were in Sarajevo, what portions of the city or it environs were controlled by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: The parts of the city under Bosnian Serb control were, of course, Grbavica, Nedzarici, and specifically Bijuvac [phoen], but now we are outside on the west, outside the city. Specifically, those places were occupied by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From the locations that you have just mentioned, would the Bosnian Serb army have had any military advantages based on its familiarity with the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, you have to know that from those places, it is clear that one can fire mortars, and that it was probably done. But those were not the best places for using mortars or for using artillery. If you are familiar with the geography and the situation of the city, the city is located in a valley and those neighbourhoods are also in the valley. Everything else is at the foot of mountains and hills, where you find the party that was besieging the city, that is the Bosnian Serbs. But from Nedzarici and Grbavica, it is clear that one can also fire mortars. What I mean is that whatever the place, from the time, from the moment that you are familiar with the place, the place where you have got to fire, once you have lived there, once you have some training, when you are a relatively well-constituted army, which was the case for the Bosnian Serbs, it is clear that the objectives like the national library, like the Old Town, like the mosque, like the market, which were symbols of the former Ottoman empire, for them, they were ideal targets. But any good military person can use that kind of weapon with precision whatever the location he is, if he is familiar with the places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commander Kolp, when you said at page 36, line 23, "Everything else is at the foot of mountains and hills where you find the party that was besieging the city, that is the Bosnian Serb," from that statement, is it correct that, in general, the Bosnian Serb army controlled the hills and mountains surrounding the city of Sarajevo during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. The city was being besieged. It was in a valley. It was surrounded by hills and mountains. So that the zone which was Ilidza, Nedzarici and Grbavica, which were enclaves, full of enclaves, in the city which was under Serb control. But the Bosnian Serbs were all around the city, around the hills, the mountains. I, myself, went by there. I met -- I encountered Serbian military people from their positions. I can assure you that you have an undisturbed view from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And maintaining positions on the high ground, coupled with a familiarity of the city, would lead to a distinct military advantage for the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: The fact that one has high positions that one can control everything that was going on, where most of the things that were going on in the town while the city was being besieged, it is clear that that would be a military advantage. There is no question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Commander Kolp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prosecution has no further questions Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms, Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kolp, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, you told us that before arriving at your mission in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, like today, that you are an army officer in the Belgian army. Could you tell us what functions you performed in the Belgian army before you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina for your mission?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Do you want to know everything from the very start of my career or just before I was assigned?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Yes, before you accepted your mission to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, right before the mission, I was in command of a company known as a specialised company within the infantry school which trains all the low ranking infantry specialists, and I was the commander of that company for two years. And at the same time, I was the chief of the military -- the military police -- the military academy of the Belgian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kolp, when you arrived in Sarajevo, you were a liaison officer, as you said, between the staff of the BH Command and the staff or the HQ of the sector of Sarajevo, the Sarajevo sector at the UN; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: That mission, that assignment, was my first assignment, yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, at the time when you arrived, which was in March 1993, who was the commander of the Sarajevo sector?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo, at the time I knew Colonel Valentin, who was finishing his mandate as the commander of the Sarajevo sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, if I say to you that the commander of the Sarajevo sector, Mr. Valentin, was on duty in July 1993, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, I can't really guarantee that Colonel Valentin stayed until July. I don't remember the time -- the date he was relieved. What I can say is that General Soubirou replaced him. Exactly when, I can't say. There was an Egyptian colonel who was the head of the staff and he had an assistant who was a negotiator, particularly, with the 1st Sarajevo Manjaca Corps. That was Debuque [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you cannot confirm with certainty that Mr. Valentin was the commander of the sector until July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No, I can't certify it just like that. I have got a lot of documentation at home. I suppose you do also, if you ask me the question, but I can't tell you just like that out of memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kolp, so you told us that your first task and your mission was to be a liaison officer between the BH command and the command of the -- the HQ of the Sarajevo sector. Could you tell us if you had a person who was your superior, and who was that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a superior. My superior, the regulatory one, the official one, was the chief of the staff, and the commander of the BH command. I would like to make it clear, however, that when you say that I was responsible for liaison between the BH command in Kiseljak and the residents in Sarajevo held the Sarajevo section, there was also a liaison mission between the BH command initially and the different parties, particularly in the Sarajevo region. By this I mean the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I asked you who was your superior. Did you have a superior and who was he? Could you tell us his name of that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, my superior to whom I reported was General Briquemont, and the Chief of Staff within the BH command, I know that there was General Hise [phoen]. There were three different ones, and I don't remember the other ones. But I do remember General Hise. But he was the chief of staff of the BH command at Sarajevo and he was detached, that is under the operational control, because we call that in military terms. I would also report to the Sarajevo sector commander. That was either Colonel Valentin or General Soubirou, depending on what period we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, your reports, your report as a liaison officer, you sent to the BH command HQ and to the HQ of the Sarajevo sector?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: What I sent as a report was transmitted, of course, in priority to the BH command. I should point out to you that that would go through the local ops, that is the operational command of the BH command in Kiseljak, in which the information was coordinated at the chief of staff level.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, your task, as you told us, was to be a liaison officer and to establish liaison between these two HQs and the three warring parties. So you had a contact with the Bosniaks, the Muslims, with the Croats and the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, to a less extent. With the HVO militia, initially, because as you must know, at the beginning of my mission, the HVO was fighting alongside the Bosnians and Muslims against the Serbs and then there was a change in alliances at a point when the HVO -- well, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't say they made an alliance with the Bosnian Serbs, but we could say that there was no longer engagement as there had been before, except for the HVO brigade in Sarajevo. And then afterwards, things turned around yet again. But I had fewer contacts with the HVO. I can tell you, however, that the liaison officers, that is the Bosnian Croats who were at the PTT building, had to leave when the alliances changed, if I can express myself that way, and were unable to get to the line -- the Bosnian Croat lines in the Kiseljak enclave through the Serbian lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kolp. Could you confirm that on the 24th and the 25th of April, 1996, you gave a statement to the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Would you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th and 25th of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, on the first page of your statement, you said that your second task that we spoke about was to establish a liaison between the two already mentioned HQs, that is the HQ of BH and the sector Sarajevo HQ, and the three warring parties, and to get the knowledge of the Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims. So you spoke of the three warring parties?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt, just for my understanding, Commander Kolp. Your testimony was that the HVO -- well, you wouldn't say that they made an alliance with the Bosnia Serbs, but you could say that there was no longer engagement with them, with the ABiH. In your next answer, you said in the English translation that the Bosnian Croats who were at the PTT building had to leave when the alliances changed, if I can express myself - these are still your words - that way, and were unable to get to the line, the Bosnian Croat line in Kiseljak through the Serbian lines. Could you explain that to me, because the prior answer suggests that there was less controversy between the Croats and the Serbs. I just try to understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right, Mr. President. When the Croats and the -- well, the Bosnian Croats and the Muslim Bosnians were fighting with one another, it is clear that at some point it was not possible for all three parties at war to fight against one another. So the common enemy for the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats were the Bosnian Muslims except in Sarajevo, where there was a special case because the HVO brigade was incorporated into the General Delic Corps, if I am not wrong. That was a very -- an inextricable situation, but that is how things happened. When I say that the liaison officers -- the Croat liaison officers were able to probably escape from prison after that change in the situations, they were in a Bosnian Muslim section in Sarajevo, that therefore of necessity they were threatened and so, through a particular strategy, they were able to get to the Bosnian Croat enclave in Kiseljak and then, in order to get out of Sarajevo, they had to go through the Serbian lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said they were "able" to. The transcript reads that they were "unable" to. That is the reason why I repeated it, and I was listening in French and was reading at the same time the English transcript. So your testimony was that when they had to leave the PTT building, that they were able to join their -- or am I wrong in understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, maybe I made a mistake here. No. They were not authorised to join up with the Croat lines, of course, but they managed to. It is clear that the Bosnian army that were in Sarajevo would not have allowed them to leave that location just by saying, "goodbye and thanks for the work that you did." They were able to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your testimony as it reads in English is that "They were unable to get..." Let me just take your own testimony. It reads: "And were unable to get to the line, the Bosnian Croat line in Kiseljak through the Serbian lines." I am not talking about authorisation, but as it reads, your testimony is that were "unable," and I now do understand that whether authorised or not, that they were able to reach their own area again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, let me state it differently. They were never authorised to leave the city by the Bosnians, that is to leave Sarajevo. But I would say probably, further to some arrangements amongst them, one of liaison officers, the Bosnian Croat liaison officers, had contacts with Major Indic and when there was this problem of changes in -- things happened and escape from Sarajevo was probably organised in order to allow them to flee the city through the Serbian lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, they managed to get there and were not unable to get there through the Serbian lines? I am not talking about authorisation but they finally got there, and as it reads in the English transcript, it seems that they finally did not manage to go through the Serbian lines to their own lines. And what you tell us now is that by whatever means, they managed to get there, but finally they got there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is right.
