And I can assure you that they were assisted, but, of course, not by the Bosnian Muslims, but they were assisted, and thanks to that assistance, they were able to join through the -- across the Serb lines without any problems. They could join up with the Kiseljak zone and afterwards to superior in Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This clarifies some confusion, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, you just told us that the Bosnian Croats from Sarajevo were not assisted by the Bosnian Muslims but that they managed to get through the Serbian positions and get to Kiseljak. Can you tell us whose assistance they had, the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You are asking me who was helping them, what assistance the Bosnian Serbs got? Is that what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No. We are talking about the Bosnia Croats who went through the Serbian areas, through the Serb-held areas.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I could answer the question, but I would have to ask the Presiding Judge. I don't know whether that can be done in open session because I think that is confidential information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although no specific protective measures have been asked for, if you think you could answer that question only in closed session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is willing to turn into closed session just for this small portion. So if that would make it easier for you to answer these questions, we will turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't mind. If could just take two minutes and then I could answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask to turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, did you have any knowledge that civilians, Serb civilians, were victims of crimes in Sarajevo, in the area of Sarajevo called Pogusevac and that there was a pit called Kazani. Did you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Honestly, I didn't know about that. It is possible but I cannot confirm that to you. I just can't. I do admit to you, honestly, that most of my time I spent -- well, that my contacts were mostly with the Bosnian Serbs. But I cannot confirm that to you. Everything was possible, but I can't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kolp, you as a liaison officer, you said yourself you had to liaise with all three warring parties, and that during direct examination, you mentioned your contacts and just now you also confirmed to us that you had many contacts with the Serbian side. Did you as the liaison officer receive protests from the warring parties that were directed to the army of the BH command and the UNPROFOR command and vice-versa? Therefore, did you receive protest that you then directed to the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No. As far as I recall, I am telling you, the part that was in the position of force was the Bosnian Serb party, which meant that the most serious problems for us, us in the UN at that time, were problems of authorisation for passage, sniping, shelling. I had four or five interventions for sniping, if not more. But a great deal for clearance. And anything that happened in the Serbian party, I could tell you -- well, I can say without hesitation, it is true I was a Belgian but I was in the UN, but I was extremely independent in my work, and it is clear that I would go out and that -- on that issue and I had to issue rules in order to get results and results specifically from the Serbs. When I say "results," it means that could bring food provisions, humanitarian assistance to the city. It was to try -- well, maybe not to adopt -- well, to get through some requests that might come from various headquarters, but mostly with the Serbs. And so my work mostly was in that zone. It is true that in the beginning I had to negotiate with the three parties, but in the end, with a few exceptions, with the HVO, 80 per cent of my work was work with the Serb side. You do know probably that, in addition, if you really wanted results, you have got to make yourself known. You have got to go speak with those people. You have got to be able -- well, otherwise you are nothing. You are not taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt again. Looking at the English transcript, I see that the testimony says that the witness had to issue rules in order to get results. But I inferred -- I think I did understand that you did not follow the rule. Is that correct? So that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I had to be outside the rules to be able to do my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just have one additional question in that respect? If you say, "I had to disobey the rules," could you give one or two examples of what the rule was and how you disobeyed them? I don't know whether you have to turn in closed session again for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. The simplest example was the UN rule which said that you could not open the window of your car when you would get to a checkpoint and had to show your ID through the window. If you did that, well, you would be blocked for four, six hours, and I would open the window. I would open the door of the car. I would go without my helmet. I would go without my bulletproof vest, without a weapon, to speak with the militia personnel at the checkpoints, in order to talk to them, to negotiate. That is something which was not authorised. When I say "go outside the rules," go outside the very well set-up rules with some discipline in which everybody has to wear the same kind of uniform. When I say "go out of the rules," that is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these are technical rules, really?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, technical rules, that's right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may continue, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kolp, you told us that on two or three occasions when there were incidents of shelling and sniping, you sent protests to Mr. Indic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I protested throughout my mandate, four or five times. Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, were these protests oral or written?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: As for me, they were always oral. When they were written protests, that was sent to me under -- in closed mail. I would send it to the postmaster and then this would be sent without really enquiring what was inside. So it would be sent to Major Indic, who was supposed to forward it to the authorities. When I received an authority, you know, the Balkan people have certain sensitivities and when the proper level is not reached -- like, coming from a general, it has to go to another general. When it comes to a Chief of Staff, it has to go to another Chief of Staff. And therefore, you have to respect the levels. I could not get mixed in with that problem. So when the General Briquemont, the BH commander, that would go to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you informed Mr. Indic on three or four occasions about shelling and sniping incidents. So can you tell us who informed you of them?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: When I, myself, went and I verbally informed Major Indic about those incidents, that most of the time it came from the operational branch of the BH command, what in military terms we called branch J-3. Maybe that came from the Sarajevo branch also, but I can tell you well, maybe it was three, four, five or six times. It wasn't very often. It ordinarily would come from the operational branch or from the duty officer. You also have to know that within the Sarajevo sector, of course there were interpreters but communication between the BH command and THE Sarajevo sector, which had a French majority, had problems, linguistic problems, because it wasn't in English, and that is what the liaison officer was used for as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you informed Mr. Indic that there is a sniping activity in a certain area of the town, and you, yourself, received this information from the operational branch of the command, can you tell us about some of these incidents of which you informed Mr. Indic, in which part of town they took place, and can you give us some further details about these incidents?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, I could. I can remember two. The first was a shelling and that was in the -- the zone that came under shelling was the Stup zone and the east side in relation to the Sarajevo Visoko, Vogosca Visoko. Therefore, the east part, there is a hill between Sarajevo, there was a hill there. We would call it Stup, the Stup forest. And that is a place which resembled more or less the shelling that had taken place during the First World War near Verdun, where all the forest had been destroyed. And the sniping took place -- well, it came from Grbavica. And I was there. I don't think that anybody was hit, but there was sniping. And as I said a little while ago, if I was the one who was being aimed at, I can tell you that had I been the target, I wouldn't be here to be talking about it now. But I was a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Kolp, you are telling us that you directed a protest to Mr. Indic, due to the shelling of the Stup area. During your mandate, did you receive information that the Stup Brdo was controlled by the BH army and that there was 102nd Motorised Brigade there?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You are asking me a lot now. But I can tell you that it is clear that that place was a strategic location, the ABiH army was in fact there, and it was an objective, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked about the protest that you sent to Mr. Indic regarding Grbavica and gave us an example that you, yourself, was also targeted by the sniper, can you tell us whether during your stay there, you ever went to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I did have the opportunity to go there twice, with a great deal of difficulty. And if I was able to get through, it was thanks to my adjudant from the Foreign Legion that spoke the language very, very well. And it wasn't because he came from there because, in fact, he came from Hungary. But he had a lot of attachments with the Serbs. And it was thanks to him that I had the opportunity to go to Grbavica two or three times, and then I was regularly prevented from going there. It was very, very difficult to access that. It was very dangerous. That is how I would answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your contact with Mr. Indic and during your conversations with him, did you ever receive protest directed to you regarding the sniping activity in the Grbavica area that originated from the other side, from the front line controlled by the BH army? Did you receive protest to the effect that snipers are shooting at Grbavica from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, no, but it is possible. But I think that you have the opportunity to ask other people. It may be that UN observers who were on site permanently at certain observation points might be able to confirm that to you. Admittedly, it is not impossible. But as far as I am concerned. I never had any complaints - I am answering your question - any complaints from Major Indic, but it is possible that there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information that in the part of the town controlled by the BH army, there was sniping shooting that originated from the town itself? Did you ever receive such information?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I don't understand your question very well. Would you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will clarify that. Did you receive information that in the part of the town that was controlled by the BH army, there existed snipers who belonged to the BH army and who were shooting throughout the town?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: What I can say that it concerns me directly and I think that I have already said, if I didn't do -- if I didn't then, it was an oversight, is that there was provocation. I mean that it is most probable, and that was stated in various reports, that at certain points it was possible, even probable, that in order to provoke or to make people believe that there had been an intervention from the Serbs, that snipers in the town, in the city, would choose as targets either equipment or people, but I don't think so. But in any case, you take as targets UN personnel, that is possible. At some points I had some doubts when I was again on the road to the airport between Stup and Kasindolska Street. At some point, I was taken at a target. It is improbable to say where it came from because there were enclaves. There was a front line which was like a snake. It is difficult to say. It is possible, and at some point, I would have said there was provocation. As regards myself, I can tell you one thing: When Major Indic told me, "Major Kolp, if you are going to go up to that line, and if you cross the line, we are going to fire on you." But so long as I never crossed that line, I was never fired on. When I did, I was fired on. So long as I didn't cross the line, I wasn't fired at. I did cross it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, according to you, as a military person, is the front zone a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry for intervening against my colleague, but this is rather important. The witness says, "We will fire on you." [French phrase] "We will fire on you," which isn't quite the same thing as "we." "On" is not the same as "we."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You heard the intervention, Commander Kolp, so I think it is more or less a request for a clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was speaking in Belgian. When Major Indic said that to me, he said "we." They would determine lines by themselves, that is very clear. It was clear. It was "we."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you interrupted Ms. Pilipovic, who was at about to ask a question. Would you please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, my question was as follows: According to you, is the front zone a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. I am sorry, but I don't think that you have asked the question very well. The front line is a line in which you have got two party -- warring parties who are confronting one another. It is clear that when one of the parties wants to gain some territory, obviously that takes place on the front line. Therefore, either the ABiH wanted to hold on to the territory, hold the ground and to hold on as long as possible and they would have to defend it, and these are assumptions. If the Bosnian Serb army were to want to take over the city, then obviously that they would be fighting at the front line, by necessity. Therefore, the front line is where the two parties come up against one another. It is a party held by both parties. That is how it happens.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, perhaps I should have asked another question prior to this one. Does the front have its depth and its length?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, the front, in this case, it had a length. I don't have a map with me, unfortunately, but if we had the chance to look at a map, you would see that there is a line which is drawn. The line goes around the town at certain points, Nedzarici, that was -- that is the front line. The line as it was determined by the UN forces and which considered to be the line at by the UN forces, but that is what we call the front line. It was at a certain depth. Depth, well, in that case, it was defence of an urban area, defence of an urban area to prevent an enemy to penetrating into that urban area and to take over the city through street combat or to prevent the enemy to take over certain strategic points like Stup, which would allow an advance, a very serious, significant advance, a breakthrough, but then you had have to have infantry. As regards to depth, I am not quite sure what you are getting at or that you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, my question concerning the length and the depth of the front is linked to my previous question, which is: Is the front in its length and depth something that we call the front zone that can be assumed to be a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, I put myself in the position as a military person on the Bosnian Serb side. If I want to take the town, of course the front line is an objective. Don't forget that the front line, as this is an inhabited area, there might be civilians there, and that is the problem. Therefore, a front zone, when you are fighting in valleys and woods, soldiers fighting soldiers, then there was no problem. But when the issue is a town where there are civilians living there and therefore who are mixed in with the soldiers defending the city, that creates problems. The front line is an objective for the party which wants to take the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke to us now about the front line or about the front zone in its depth and length and also spoke about street combat or urban combat, do you believe that it is allowed to have civilians reside in the front zone?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Listen, when you have 400.000, 500.000 people living in the city and from one day to the next, or almost one day to the next, is being besieged, are you going to put all the people in a stadium and wait for a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shell to hit the stadium? That is not a solution. You can't put 400.000 or 500.000 people outside the city. And those people who are in the city, they had an objective, to defend their positions against the enemy which wanted to take this town. Sarajevo, I know, was by necessity also a symbol in the eyes of the international community. Therefore, it was resistance against the aggressor, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague is telling me that there is a problem in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness spoke about people in general who were in the -- remained in the city, who wanted to defend their positions. That is not in the transcript. It must have not been included in the transcript; it wasn't picked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked to ask you Commander Kolp, to repeat perhaps the part just referred to by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so that it will appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You want me to repeat what I just said; is that what you are asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you might have noticed that Mr. Piletta-Zanin has referred to that part of your answer that people in general who were in the remaining -- who were -- I think it was remaining in the city and wanted to defend their positions. That was part of your answer. But I have some difficulties in reconstructing it, as a matter of fact. But do you recall that part where you were referring to the people in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that the people wanted to remain to defend their city, the inhabitants don't want to leave their tone. And so the civilian population, for the most part, wanted to remain in the town and to get back to what they call a normal situation. Clearly, Sarajevo was the largest centre occupied with a -- by Bosnian Muslims. And there were military forces, in this case, the ABiH army, defending the city. But when I say that inhabitants wanted to defend their city, inhabitants wanted to stay in their town, as my -- that is my interpreter who didn't want to leave there because he was born there because that is what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, looking at the clock, I know it is time approximately to have a break. I don't know whether this would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we can have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I nevertheless noted that I am violating my own suggestions. May I just ask one question relating to the testimony up to this point. When asked by Ms. Pilipovic on the -- whether the front lines or the front zone would be an acceptable military target, you repeatedly stated that it -- of course you had to attack the front line of the front zone if you wanted to take the city, or as you said, "on devait prendre la ville," would your answer be the same if one of the parties who did not intend to gain any ground would fire at those at the front line, those from the other party at the front line? I mean, how important is that part of your answer which states that it would be an acceptable military target if you want to take the city? Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that the witness is having some difficulty was listening to the French interpretation, because maybe we don't have enough detail. Perhaps we could ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...[Interpretation] Let me ask the question in French. It is not easy for me but I will try. You answered and part of your answer was "that the front line or the front zone was a military target when you want to take the town." What is the significance of that last part of your answer? Does that mean when you don't want to take the town or when you don't want to progress or gain ground, would firing even on soldiers who are in the front line or the front zone, would that also be a military target, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion, Your Honour is, first, that every front line is an objective, a target, for the person seeking together further. In this particular case of a town, where there are civilians, a city under siege as this one was, it is unquestionable that if there were military people fighting there, then that is a front line with soldiers attacking and defending it. But at the point that there was civilians living in that zone and who are not parties because they have no choice that the enemy, that is if the enemy -- the besieging doesn't leave them a choice. It is difficult to say that that is a military objective. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer then depends only on the presence of civilians? When one does not intend to gain ground, that is, when there is a front, a stable front line, when -- well, there would be many reasons for not wanting to move forward. Does that mean that the people -- those who were on the front line were of military objective? Is it permissible to attack them even if one does not want to change the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If one does not want to change the line, if you want to maintain it, there is no reason for it to be a military target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your answer. [In English] I know that I am to blame for having a late break. We will have a break until a quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 6.17 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, when you were talking about the front zone, do you have any knowledge on whether during your stay in Sarajevo, was it -- were the civilians banned from leaving the city of Sarajevo by the authorities in Sarajevo in the area under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I think so. I think so, and the reason was -- the question was asked and the reason given was that it was better for their safety to stay in the city than to risk being killed crossing the front line. But I think that it was the civilian population was advised not to leave the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, when we are talking about the city of Sarajevo, could you tell us whether you know how many municipalities made up the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I did know it. I had a lot of maps. At the time I knew, and in the next two years I might have been able to answer, but now it is more difficult for me. I could tell you that there was Kosnorici [phoen], Sergonici [phoen], Boskic [phoen]. There are others, but I really could not right now tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, if I tell you that parts of the city of Sarajevo under the control of the army of Republika Srpska were parts of the city called Grbavica, Rajlovac, Alija, Vogosca, Ilijas, Hadzici, Pale, and Trnovo, would you agree with me that these were the parts of the city of Sarajevo that were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Let me tell you the following: As a former UN person, the so-called Republika Srpska, because it was not recognised officially, this has to be known, of course, Ilidza, yes, of course, but when I talk about the city, Ilidza, yes, it is part of greater Sarajevo, yes. Ilidza was right after the Stup bridge. Rajlovac, the part which was to the west Rajlovac, Vogosca road, up to a certain part in the west was under Serb control. And when one got a little further and one would take the road to the east, the right, where there was a weapons factory, that was completely in the Serbian section. Ilidza was the same thing, Hadzici, of course. Blazuj, Hadzici, yes, yes, that is right. Yes, I agree absolutely with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, would you agree with me if we analysed the parts of Sarajevo that were under the control of the BH army and the parts of the city that were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, would you agree with me if I said that Sarajevo was a divided city?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, I could agree with you when you used the word "divided" or"` shared" but absolutely not in identical proportions. You know that the neighbourhoods to a large degree outside where the municipalities were to a very large extent outside or on the very edges of what one could call the Sarajevo entity. Of course, that was under VRS control. But I can see that when in the centre of the city, perhaps which you are familiar with, which had between 400.000 and 500.000 inhabitants, it is difficult -- well, yes, divided, yes. But not proportion -- not a 50-50 division. Proportionally, yes, but not 50-50.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "50-50" and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, we have heard a lot of testimony about what parts were under control of the Bosnian Serb forces and what parts of the municipality and the town were under the control of the opposing forces. What is the use of asking the witness whether it was a divided city? I mean, of course, we get the answer we could all imagine that we could get. The relevance is totally unclear. It is a matter of opinion. I would rather stick to the facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the relevance of this question is in the answer that Mr. Kolp gave when he was answering the question of the Defence. He was talking about the aggressors. And my question was phrased regarding this particular word. So the reason why I would ask the question whether Mr. Kolp would agree with me whether part of Grbavica was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice that he used the word "aggressor" but not as a term far, as far as I remember, but we could look it up, but that he considered one part the aggressor but that this was felt by the population a such. That was my recollection, but I could easily look it up. So -- but please proceed. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- ask the witness why he thinks that one party is the aggressor. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I was meaning to ask this question, Mr. Kolp. When you were talking about the population and that they believed that one side was the aggressor, could you clarify this for us? Could you tell us which side did this or whether both sides, looking at a divided city, believed that the other side was the aggressor. So the question of aggression and the attitude of the population.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: The point of view of the population and possibly my own -- well, not mine, the population: First of all, when I was in the city and again in a city under siege, without water, without electricity, without food or medicine, 400.000 to 500.000 civilians, for them, the aggressor was the people besieging the city and preventing the entrance of all food and other provisions, medicine included. When I talk about the Serbs, or the Serb side, when I talk about with Serbs, and some of them I got along very well. There are good people everywhere. They would tell me, "There is nothing to be done. I think it is a question of history." And the Serbian people know its history and the Serb people has never digested, and I have frequently referred to me -- they spoke about invasions, the Ottoman invasions and what happened at that time, and they thought that that territory was Bosnian, well, that the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was theirs, and that for the entire Serb people. And they told me that Milosevic said this: Milosevic says, "I would say that the population -- the majority of the Serbian population I met would say that where there is one Serb, I consider that that is Serbian territory." That is it. Period.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, did you speak to the population of Grbavica, Nedzarici, and Ilidza? Was this population also suffering the fact that there was no electricity, water or medicines?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: It is clear, to be completely honest, that Grbavica once again, I told you, it is on the front line, the situation was not bearable for the civilians, whatever their ethnic group was. That is clear. I am not going to say the opposite, because you wouldn't believe me if I did. As regards Nedzarici, I think that is the same thing because it was a Serb enclave of people who were relatively isolated, even though they did have some regular contacts with Lukavica. Because by necessity there were orders that had to be given. But I did not have any contact with Grbavica. But when you would go out of those two very specific neighbourhoods, and there I agree with you, when you would go out and you would go on the Serb side, I would say that you would get -- you would find everything you wanted. There was meat. Anything. Everything you wanted. Maybe not all the necessary medicines, and that is why the humanitarian organisations agreed to share when the Serb authority would grant passage, there was a proportional distribution of medicines and dialysis machines. A part would go to the Serbs and part would go to the centre of the town of Sarajevo. But I am now answering your question honestly that it must not have been very good in Grbavica or Nedzarici, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kolp, when you were answering the question asked by my learned colleague about the artillery emplacements and the mortar positions, you said that the Serbs had an advantage, and you also said that under control -- or that hills and mountains were under the control of the Republika Srpska; is that correct, in relation to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes. In the majority of the controlled zones, the heights were controlled by the VRS. As regards weapons, it is clear, you know, all reports say that. All the observers say it. I saw the reports, and I don't think that you could deny the fact that in respect of tanks and artillery - I didn't mention rocket launchers - that's artillery, tanks -- tanks and artillery, the VRS was unquestionably superior. You can't ask me how many pieces of equipment there was. I think the reports would say that. You could find that without any problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, you personally, during your stay and your mandate in Sarajevo, did you visit Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, I had the opportunity to travel to various locations. For instance, I had the opportunity to go on several times to Pale via the Lukavica road. And when I said a while ago that we had a superb view of the city, there were Serb positions, there were people with rifles which we called sniper rifles. That is in every army. I didn't see them firing, I can tell you that right off. I had the opportunity see artillery positions and tanks. Unfortunately, I never went to the north side of Sarajevo -- maybe that is the other side of the front line, but I did have the opportunity to go to Rajlovac, it was dangerous. To go across the bridge to go to Visiko, where it was also extremely dangerous, and where I did see artillery pieces and tanks. I saw artillery pieces in Ilidza near the Roman bridge, a artillery piece which was directed at the city at 130 millimetres, and the team that was firing shots, that I did see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, as you were now talking about the positions of the army of Republika Srpska, that you went to Pale and Rajlovac and Ilidza, during your stay, did you visit the positions of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I would have to tell you honestly that I had less -- fewer occasions to go because 80 per cent of my work was to liaise between the parties. But I worked much more -- I was too busy with the Serb side. So I did have the opportunity to see certain of the ABiH positions. They also had some mortars, some artillery pieces, not much, but they did have some. I spoke to you about provocations. There were provocations. I am not denying that. And when the Bosnian Serbs fired on the Kosevo hospital, it is clear that at least on one occasion a mortar position fired from that hospital on to Serb positions. That did happen. I am Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. honest and frank with you. But, ultimately, what are the proportions that we have to accept?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, you were now telling us about the positions of the Republika Srpska army and the BH army positions. In your statement, on page 6, you said that the army of Republika Srpska had some military targets around Sarajevo and you were talking about the Zuc hill, Zuc mountain. Could you tell us is Zuc a mountain or a hill that was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is Zuc. There were military forces of the ABiH and, yes, those forces -- well, I told you that was a strategic point. It was a place which was frequently shelled by the Serb artillery. It was a military target.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, would you agree with me that in the part of the city of Sarajevo under the army of BH, there was Stup hill and Brijesce hill and Mojmilo hill and Hum hill and the hills Colina, Kapa Velika and Mala, so in the period from March 1993 to October 1994, were these hills that in that period were under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Honestly, if you were to show me a map, I could answer. But I just can't answer out of my head like that without a map. I know that you must feel that is extremely important if you are asking me that question, but I don't remember all those places eight years afterwards. I would have to look at some maps. I can't remember things just like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to request, with your leave, if the witness can be shown a map. This is the map that we have used here before, of my learned colleagues from the Prosecution. I believe that is the map 3644.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, Ms. Pilipovic, I would like to understand the answer of the witness well. He said, "It is eight years ago; I couldn't do it without a map." Did he mean a blank map where he could indicate exactly during this period where the -- well, which hill was under the control of which party or would he mean, I don't know, that he would need a map with already the findings of that time illustrated on it. It is not quite clear to me, giving him a blank map, if he couldn't draw it on, that seems to be rather useless. But I am not quite sure about his position. Mr. Kolp, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is clear that on site we had maps on which the front line, which it changed from time to time, was indicated and on which the positions were also marked. This is the kind of map that we worked with over a period of two years. I think that at some point or another they might have been available to the Tribunal or to another authority. They were UN maps. That type of map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be able to reproduce the front lines or at least those part of the hills under control by which party, if you would be given a blank map, just hills on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could try. I can't guarantee the results, but I am willing to try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you are willing to make an observation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, we would object on the grounds that we have much evidence adduced with respect of various locations, hills, mountains and front lines, during the course of the trial. Simply, we object on the grounds that it is accumulative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would it be any use to give the witness a chance to see what he could reproduce, if there is a lot of evidence already on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to have the map shown to the witness so that we can check how -- to what extent the witness can find his bearings on a map and to point the location that he is certain about on the map, and I would also like to ask the question about the mountains. Mr. Kolp said that mountains were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Perhaps the witness would be able to tell us about Mount Igman and under whose control was it while he was on his -- on his duty in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is just a global matter, Ms. Pilipovic, first of all, do you have any unmarked copies of the map with you and available to the Court as well so that we can follow the testimony? I mean, just showing the one we have would not be enough. We would need to have a blank copy of this map as well. We should. Of course, as you know, we always follow the testimony of the witness by writing on it as well. But perhaps if you could say -- if you could just mention a few hills, that perhaps we would find out whether the witness is aware of it. You started already with Mount Igman. So I don't want to interrupt you. But if you insist on using the map, of course, you should have brought one, copies for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment, I don't have an unmarked map because we agreed that we would be using one map for the witnesses, that is, the map that was used by my learned colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need clean copies in order to follow the markings of the witness, but let me just first confer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, the Defence will not insist on having the map shown to the witness because since it is a question of how much the witness will be able to tell us, and we would not like to waste any more time, I can ask a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...on questions without using a map. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. I also note that there is not much time left for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, do you know or would you agree with me, in fact, that Mount Igman was under the control of the BH army while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No, I don't agree completely in the sense that I wanted to be clear that when we talk about Igman, for me, that represents the entire mountain chain near -- above the village of Butmir. Maybe I am wrong because there is Bjelasnica on the other side. However, to tell you that I still have the sense of direction, when you leave there, you have the airport road, which was closed from Kazindolska, up to the part under Serb control. A little bit further going now toward Vojdmir [phoen] and then to the right of the road driving to the Serb side is the airport. On the extension of the -- from the airport moving toward Igman is the village of Hrasnica and the village of Butmir, if my geography is right. And then after Butmir, there is a road which goes up toward Igman and which made it possible to join Pazarici and the road from Tarcin in order to get to Konarc [phoen]. That was under the ABiH army control, but I went further than that. I went further. I went up, much further toward Trnovo to the mountains, and there I saw Serb troops that were withdrawing and -- well, and burning the villages. So there was fighting. I did not witness the fighting. I saw the withdraw, that is, the policy of the scorched earth. I might have mentioned it when I talk about the heights there. That part of what I call "Igman" was under ABiH control and that is how I got up my clandestine convoys and that is why I am so familiar with that region. And I came out of the roads by following those -- out of the lines by following the roads. But if you go too far to the right, that is, too much to the east, you would get to Blazuj. And if you went too much to the west, I would again be in Serb zone. But you are right. You go too far to the right, that is too much. There the ABiH was under the control and it was the only possible road for the ABiH to bring in ammunition, weapons and supplies. Along that road, up to [inaudible] and to go through the tunnel because now everyone knows there was a tunnel. At the time, you couldn't say so, but now you can, and to get into the city, yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kolp, you are telling us that across Mount Igman to Sarajevo, on the way to Sarajevo, through the tunnel under the airport, there were weapons that were transported for the BH army in Sarajevo in the part of town that was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, well, I don't know if you had the opportunity to visit that tunnel. You know, when I say, "tunnel" it is not a tunnel as we think of a tunnel in our own language. When I say, "tunnel" that is something practical. There, a tunnel was a mine tunnel. And that was the way that the wounded would be brought out for treatment outside. And it's true that that is how the small amount -- the small arms and food was sent was possible, that could be transported, and that was how that would go through, running many risks. But I do agree with you, these weapons were used by the defenders of the city, yes, by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, would you agree with me that the 1st Corps of the BH army in the part of town under the control of the BH army, was comprised of 11 brigades?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: That is possible. That is quite possible. But I think that -- when we talk about brigades, that is not the equivalent of the brigade what we have in our countries. In our countries, there are infantry regimens, there are brigades. Their brigade could be 200 men. It is possible, very possible. I don't remember, but it is possible that in the first army, I don't know whether that was General Delic or General Divjak or someone else who was in command, but it is very possible there were 11 brigades, but that is relative.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, could you tell us about the BH army in Sarajevo. Were all members -- did all members of the BH army had uniforms or were there uniforms apart -- uniforms in part civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Not everybody was wearing a standard uniform. Why? As I said to you, all those who were of fighting age apparently to defend the city - I don't want to speak about military targets - they bore arms, had to bear arms in order to defend the city. Now, I can assure you that with that type of a siege, and the Yugoslav army, which was still at the barracks, they brought everything with them to find uniforms or to make uniforms for all the fighters from one day to the next. Whereas the town was under siege, I think that would be typical. So to answer your question, I would say, no, not everybody was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, when you answer the question, it often happens that you are also giving your opinion on whether it would have been difficult to given uniforms or not. The question was just whether they were wearing uniforms or civilian clothes. May I ask you to perhaps keep it a bit more strict to the facts and listen carefully to the questions. Ms. Pilipovic, I know that I took one minute of your time, but you are already close to the same time as examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to finish my cross-examination soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, would you agree with me that in the part of town under the control of the BH army, as we were talking now about uniforms and how BH army was dressed, was it difficult to tell civilians and soldiers apart? You can just answer by "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolp, when you were telling us today during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned the destruction of cultural buildings. Could you tell us how many mosques were destroyed in Sarajevo, do you know, since you were telling us about mosques?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned colleague has -- my learned colleague would like to ask two questions, with your leave, and then we would finish the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Two questions. I will allow two questions. That means the first question is the first one and the second question is the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, witness. Did you ever hear or speak about General Galic? Did you ever hear him giving orders in terms of snipers?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you hear General Galic give any type of orders about shelling?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No need for re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No need for re-direct. That brings me to another issue - we have to strictly finish at 7.00 today - whether there are any questions from the Bench? Judge Nieto-Navia would like to put one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like "yes" or "no" answers, please. When you spoke about paramilitaries, you said, and now I am quoting, "They were not soldiers because a soldier wears or has a uniform." You said that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the Bosnian Serb army, by -- through military intimidation, attacked the PTT building. You said that?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many times?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Twice, maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, that is all.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has also one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As regards what you call "paramilitaries," you said that these are uncontrollable elements. What exactly do you mean by "uncontrollable"? Does that mean that they were not subject to the commands of the military hierarchy? Were they volunteers doing what he wanted? Or were they part of a global strategy?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: In my opinion, they were part of an overall strategy. Despite everything, they were elements -- I don't say uncontrollable, but not controlled or difficult -- controlled with difficulty. They would work -- they would act on their own accord, but when an issue was an operation of a greater scope, they were also involved in the operation. But I can assure you that those elements could do certain things without the hierarchy being aware of everything going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Still, they did fall under the command of the army, that is the impression you have?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: As regards the Bosnian Serb army, it was an army where -- where the well-established chain of command, a very rigid one, which did not accept any kind of the discussions and which demanded, in my opinion, to be informed about what was going on, and that is why probably those people, those groups, moved to Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as regards to their authority, their main jurisdiction encompassed, do you know what it is they did?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, I was never in direct contact with those people. They were the types of groups, they were extreme nationalists who are prepared Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to do anything they can do in order to destroy the enemy, whether that enemy is a civilian or military. That, in my opinion, is the difference between them and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spoke about a shelling which targeted the library.

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you assert the origin of that of that shelling, from which army?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, I myself did not witness this, but on several occasions, I saw reports on STV, which was a Bosnian Serb propaganda, in where you see General Mladic giving orders, in Serbo-Croat, that was translated for the staff, as the people who were in charge of the Sarajevo sector, and it was translated by -- not by local translators, but by the official translator of the General and, apparently, General Mladic himself in person directed that manoeuvre and ordered that shots be fired on the old city and the library. Those orders came from General Mladic. Ordinarily, it was the supreme command of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did those orders go through the military hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, I assume that General Mladic when he would say to one of his assistants - I don't know which one, one of those who was with him - "Go ahead." When he would say "go ahead," by definition, it was the chain of command. But what that chain of command was, I don't know. Did Mladic give the orders himself to his battle commanders to fire, I don't know. It is difficult to say, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps one final question. You said that it was a well-trained army. In your opinion, the professionalism and this training, did it allow the army to target a market surrounded by buildings with a single shot? Because we did hear testimony, according to which, for such a fire, there had to be two or three. So with one shot, can one say that in light of the professionalism of that army, could it hit a market?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: I think so. However, I do have to tell you that for a long time there was some hesitations about who had fired because it came from the front line. And so -- well, that is my second question, in fact. Now, when it comes to telling you that an artillery person, a Serb, that it was a Serb, it would be very difficult. I can say it was not the only shot. If it was just a shot on to the market, one would have to be a very skilled specialist. But there were several previous shots on to the city. So the shooting plans were well-established. I can tell you this: In terms of artillery, they were very experienced specialists and, of course, you would need a team capable of being so exact in order to shoot that way. Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion, the direction from where the fire originated, these positions were under the control of what party?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: Well, you know, when you talk about the front line, if you put yourself to the -- well, the shell was fired from the north of Sarajevo, not far from Markovici, around there, maybe a little bit more to the south or front line. If you are south of the front line, you have Bosnian positions. If you are north of the front line, on the other side, then those were the Bosnian Serb positions. Now, as a military person, if I am right south of the front line, what would I do with 120 millimetre mortar near the front line in order to fire on soldiers right on the other side, not very far away? I think that, in military terms, that wouldn't be so justified. Or perhaps in order to fire in other targets that were further away, I wouldn't be able to tell you that. Therefore, in my opinion, it is more likely that the shot was fired from the front line, but from the Serb side, probably. I emphasise it was probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question is: You spoke about firing coming from the Kosevo hospital. Was that before or after the hospital was targeted by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JACQUES CHARLES LEON KOLP
utterances.text: You know, it was a kind of cat and mouse game. The hospital had already been fired on. You know, all you need is one time in order to put -- on a single occasion, a mortar position from the ABiH was installed there in order to say, "Well, you see, they are even firing from the hospital without having it -- without being seen." But once it has been done once in one's mind they would say, "Well, why wouldn't they do it several times?" But I would say that, according to UN sources, the hospital had already been shot on several times but not destroyed, Your Honour, but several shots had been fired from the Serb side. But, you know, that is always a very difficult game to define specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question? Your travel arrangements, are they such that you would leave this evening or by tomorrow? I am just wondering --- we wanted to stop strictly at 7.00. We didn't manage to do that. I have a few question, not many, to you. Was it intended that you leave today or would you stay anyhow until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When I came here I was planning to do what had to be done. So if you like, I will be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am just wondering, do you intend to travel back home this evening or -- ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, may I ask you, I want to take into consideration your position as well, and it will only be for a very short time, but, nevertheless, I will have to ask you to come back tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00, since we had to stop as a matter of fact at 7.00. And it is already 10 minutes past 7.00. So may I also thank especially the interpreters because I did not ask their specific permission to continue for 10 minutes. Thank you very much for your cooperation. We will adjourn until tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th, day of May, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
